P1.title: Prima Pars (First Part): God and Creation
P1.bookSummary:
The Prima Pars opens the Summa by asking what sacred doctrine itself is: a science distinct from philosophy because it proceeds from principles known by divine revelation rather than by natural light alone, yet one that freely employs philosophical reasoning as a handmaid in the service of truths that exceed unaided reason. Having secured this methodological footing, Aquinas turns immediately to God's existence, rejecting both the claim that it is self-evident and the claim that it is indemonstrable, and offering the five ways—arguments from motion, efficient causality, contingency, the gradation of perfections, and the governance of the world—as proofs accessible to natural reason.

The bulk of the part is then devoted to what can be known of the divine nature itself. Aquinas proceeds negatively before he proceeds positively: God is shown to be simple (without composition of matter and form, essence and existence, genus and difference), perfect, infinite, unchangeable, one, and incorporeal. Only after establishing this apophatic foundation does he treat God's positive attributes—knowledge (including God's knowledge of singulars and of future contingents), the ideas in the divine mind, truth and falsity, life, will, love, justice and mercy, providence, and the fullness of divine power, culminating in the question of whether God can do what is absolutely impossible.

The treatise on the Trinity follows, examining the processions of the divine Persons (the Word proceeding by way of intellect, the Holy Spirit by way of will and love), the relations that distinguish Father, Son, and Spirit without dividing the one divine essence, and the propriety of the persons and their notional acts—material that depends entirely on revelation and could not be reached by philosophy alone.

The part then turns from God considered in Himself to God as Creator. Aquinas treats creation as the production of being from nothing, distinguishes it from natural change, and examines the six days of creation described in Genesis, harmonizing the literal account with philosophical cosmology. A substantial treatise on the angels follows—their nature as subsistent forms without matter, their knowledge, will, and hierarchical order, and the fall of the rebel angels—before Aquinas turns to the corporeal creation and, finally, to man.

The treatise on man is among the most influential sections of the entire Summa: the human being is a single substance composed of a rational soul as substantial form and body as matter, made in the image of God precisely through intellect and will. Aquinas examines the soul's powers, how the intellect abstracts universal knowledge from sensory phantasms, the relation of intellect to will, and the state of the first human beings before the fall. The Prima Pars closes with the government of creatures by divine providence, setting up the ordered universe—God, angels, the physical cosmos, and man—within which the moral and salvific drama of the rest of the Summa unfolds.

P2.title: Prima Secundae (First Part of the Second Part): Human Acts and Virtues
P2.bookSummary:
The Prima Secundae shifts the Summa's attention from God as the origin of creation to man's return to God through his own acts, and it opens by declaring that man's last end is happiness—a beatitude that cannot consist in wealth, honor, fame, power, bodily good, pleasure, or any created thing, but only in the vision of the divine essence itself. Everything that follows in this part is organized around the question of how human acts are ordered, or fail to be ordered, toward that end.

Aquinas first analyzes the human act as such: what makes an act voluntary, how ignorance, violence, and fear can render an act involuntary or diminish its voluntariness, and how the will and reason interact in choice, consent, and use. He then examines the passions of the soul in careful psychological detail—love and hatred, desire and aversion, joy and sorrow, hope and despair, fear and daring, and anger—treating them not as mere disturbances but as movements of the sensitive appetite that can be rightly ordered by reason.

From acts and passions the treatise moves to the more stable principles that dispose a person toward good or evil: habits in general, and then virtue as a good habit that perfects a power of the soul. Aquinas distinguishes intellectual, moral, and theological virtues, and organizes the moral virtues around the four cardinal virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—that between them govern practical reason, the will in relation to others, and the passions of aggression and desire. Vice and sin receive equally systematic treatment as privations and disorders opposed to virtue, including the causes of sin in ignorance, weakness, malice, and the passions, and the distinction between mortal and venial sin.

The part also contains Aquinas's mature treatise on law, arguing that law is an ordinance of reason for the common good, and distinguishing eternal law (God's own rational plan for the universe), natural law (the rational creature's participation in the eternal law, known through the first principles of practical reason), human law (positive law derived from natural law), and divine law (revealed law, given because human law alone cannot perfectly direct man to his supernatural end). The Prima Secundae closes with an extended treatise on grace—its necessity, its nature as a supernatural gift elevating human nature, and its relation to merit—establishing that no one can attain the beatitude described at the outset by natural powers alone, but only through grace working with a free and rightly ordered will.

P3.title: Secunda Secundae (Second Part of the Second Part): Virtues and Moral Conduct
P3.bookSummary:
Where the Prima Secundae treated the general principles of morality, the Secunda Secundae applies them in exhaustive detail to the concrete virtues by which particular kinds of human conduct are rightly ordered—making it by far the longest part of the Summa. It opens with the three theological virtues. Faith is examined as an assent of the intellect commanded by the will under the influence of grace, together with the sins opposed to it (unbelief, heresy, apostasy) and the gift of understanding that accompanies it. Hope is treated as the virtue by which one trusts in the attainment of eternal beatitude through God's help, opposed by both despair and presumption. Charity, the greatest of the virtues, is examined as friendship with God grounded in the communication of His own beatitude, extending to love of neighbor, and opposed by hatred, sloth, envy, and discord; the treatise also considers the precepts of charity and the order of charity itself, and closes with a treatment of the religious life as a school of charity.

The cardinal virtues then receive equally thorough treatment, each examined together with its integral, subjective, and potential parts and the vices and sins opposed to it. Prudence—right reason applied to action—is analyzed alongside its counterfeits (cunning, negligence, inconstancy) and its allied virtues of counsel and foresight. Justice occupies the largest single treatise in the whole Summa: commutative justice governing exchange between individuals, distributive justice governing the common good, and their many derivative virtues and vices, including extended discussions of theft, murder, lying, detraction, restitution, and the duties owed to God through religion (adoration, devotion, prayer, sacrifice, and the vices of superstition and irreligion), as well as extensive treatment of law-related topics such as judgment, and social questions including usury.

Fortitude and its parts—including patience, perseverance, and the willingness to face martyrdom—are examined next, followed by temperance and its many subordinate virtues: abstinence, sobriety, chastity, continence, meekness, and humility, along with their opposed vices such as gluttony, lust, and pride. Throughout, Aquinas correlates each virtue with a corresponding gift of the Holy Spirit, showing how the infused gifts perfect virtue beyond what unaided human effort could achieve.

The part concludes by considering the different states and vocations of Christian life: the distinction between the active life (engaged in temporal and charitable works) and the contemplative life (devoted to the knowledge and love of God), with Aquinas arguing that the contemplative life is simply the higher of the two though the active life may sometimes be preferable in particular circumstances; and finally the specific states of perfection within the Church—bishops, religious, and those bound by vows—each examined for how it orders a person toward the perfection of charity.

P4.title: Tertia Pars (Third Part): Christ and the Sacraments
P4.bookSummary:
Having shown in the first two parts that man's last end is beatitude and that virtue and grace are needed to reach it, Aquinas devotes the Tertia Pars to Christ as the way by which that end is actually attained—"since our Savior the Lord Jesus Christ, in saving His people from their sins, showed unto us in His own Person that way of truth whereby we may attain to the bliss of eternal life." The part opens with the fittingness and manner of the Incarnation: why it was fitting for God to become man, whether the Incarnation would have occurred apart from sin, and the mode of union of the divine and human natures. Aquinas defends the orthodox formula of one divine Person subsisting in two complete natures against the ancient Christological errors, examining what it means for Christ to have a true human body, a true human soul, and two complete wills and operations, one divine and one human, united without confusion in the single Person of the Word.

From the metaphysics of the union, the treatise turns to what belongs to Christ in virtue of that union: His grace as man (both the personal grace of His individual holiness and His capital grace as head of the Church), His knowledge (beatific, infused, and acquired), His power, and the defects He freely assumed—including bodily weaknesses, hunger, weariness, and death itself—so as to be a true and sufficient Redeemer. Aquinas then narrates and analyzes Christ's earthly life and saving work: His conception and nativity, His baptism and temptation, His teaching and miracles, and above all His Passion, examining its causes, its bitterness, and its efficient causality as at once a meritorious act, a sacrifice, a redemption, and a satisfaction of infinite worth precisely because offered by a divine Person. The treatise continues through Christ's descent to the dead, resurrection, appearances, and ascension, and His session at the right hand of the Father, from which He will come to judge the living and the dead.

The part then turns to the sacraments as the instrumental causes by which Christ's grace won on the Cross is applied to individual believers across time. After a general treatise on sacramental causality, number, and effects, Aquinas examines each sacrament in turn: Baptism, which incorporates a person into Christ and remits original and actual sin; Confirmation, which strengthens the baptized for spiritual combat; and the Eucharist, treated at exceptional length and depth, covering the reality of Christ's substantial presence under the appearances of bread and wine, transubstantiation, the sacrament's effects, and its proper administration and reception. Aquinas's own text breaks off partway through the treatise on Penance—the Tertia Pars was left unfinished at his death—but even in its incomplete state it develops a rich theology of contrition, confession, and satisfaction as the means by which sins committed after Baptism are forgiven, before turning toward the remaining sacraments of healing and vocation that complete the Church's sacramental life.
